title: 1992 onwards: from noodle bar to mainstream
body:
From 1992 a handful of founders, almost none of them Japanese, turned Japanese food from an expatriate niche into a British high-street habit. They did it by selling a format rather than a cuisine: the canteen noodle bar, the conveyor belt and the sushi box to take back to your desk. Private equity then paid for the roll-out, and the biggest brands changed hands several times. In 2023 one of them was bought by a Japanese company, which closed a circle that began with Japanese firms' arrival in lesson 3.

### The starting point

In the 1980s Japanese restaurants in London were mostly discreet places in the City, St James's and Mayfair, used by Japanese businessmen, plus grocers near the Japanese schools (lesson 3). They were expensive, and to most Britons sushi meant raw fish they had not tried. The importers and fishmongers serving Japanese families were already in place. What was missing was a format a British customer would walk into without knowing the menu.

### Wagamama: the noodle bar as a format

Alan Yau opened the first Wagamama in Bloomsbury in 1992. The company had been incorporated in April 1991 as China Diner Limited ([Wikipedia: Wagamama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagamama)). Yau has said the idea came from his time with McDonald's in Hong Kong, and that the menu was based on ramen ([South China Morning Post](https://scmp.com/article/718802/alan-yau)).

The design did as much work as the food. [Campaign](https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/wagamama/1135761) describes an open kitchen, a minimalist refectory-style dining room, fast service and shared benches with strangers. No bookings, quick turnover and a short menu kept the cost per meal down. The first site, on Streatham Street, closed on 19 June 2016 (Wikipedia).

Yau left early. Sources differ on whether he lost control in 1997 to the venture capitalists who funded the expansion or sold in 1998, when there were two sites. I use 1997, the year given on his own Wikipedia page ([Wikipedia: Alan Yau](https://www.Wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Yau)). The chain kept growing under a run of financial owners, covered below. It took no table bookings until this year.

### 1994 to 1997: sushi goes on a belt

Kaiten-zushi (回転寿司), conveyor-belt sushi, lets diners pick plates as they pass and pay by plate colour. It is cheap to staff and needs no menu knowledge.

1. **Moshi Moshi, 1994.** Caroline Bennett, who had lived in Japan, opened it at Liverpool Street station. It is usually described as Britain's first conveyor-belt sushi restaurant ([Network Rail](https://property.networkrail.co.uk/news-help-and-insights/case-studies/celebrating-30-years-of-moshi-moshi/)). That claim comes from the company and is repeated by others; I found no independent check. Moshi Moshi stayed small, and is better known for sustainable fish sourcing.
2. **YO! Sushi, 22 January 1997.** Simon Woodroffe opened in Poland Street, Soho, with £200,000 of his own savings ([YO!](https://yo.co.uk/simon-woodroffe/)). He added call buttons, robot drinks trolleys and Japanese television. The theatre, not the fish, was the selling point.

### Sushi to go: itsu and Wasabi

The other route was the lunch box. Julian Metcalfe had co-founded Pret a Manger with Sinclair Beecham in 1986, and founded itsu in 1997 ([Wikipedia: Julian Metcalfe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Metcalfe)). itsu applied Pret's grab-and-go model, food packed in the morning and bought in under a minute, to sushi, salads and noodle soups.

itsu later moved into supermarkets. Its grocery range, at first part of Metcalfe's Food Company, became part of itsu in 2015. In the year to 1 January 2026 itsu's revenue rose 14.1% to £201 million, and grocery sales rose 33% to £75.8 million, while restaurant revenue grew only 2.8% ([City AM via search](https://www.cityam.com/itsu-return-to-the-office-helps-boost-sales/)). Over a third of the brand's sales now come from shops it does not run.

Wasabi, founded in London in 2003 by the South Korean entrepreneur Dong Hyun Kim, did the same with sushi and hot bento boxes. It had 36 UK sites in 2014 and 47 by March 2022 ([Wikipedia: Wasabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasabi_(restaurant))).

### The high end

The top of the market developed in parallel, also largely without Japanese owners. Nobu, the partnership of chef Matsuhisa Nobuyuki and Robert De Niro, opened on Old Park Lane in the late 1990s ([Business Traveller](https://www.businesstraveller.com/features/sushi-selection/)). I could not confirm the exact year in a source this run. Zuma opened in Knightsbridge in 2002, founded by the German chef Rainer Becker, who had spent six years running the kitchens of the Park Hyatt in Tokyo, and Arjun Waney ([Wikipedia: Zuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuma_(restaurant))). Zuma is modelled on the izakaya (居酒屋), a Japanese pub serving shared plates, dressed up for a luxury crowd. Lesson 5 looks at this tier.

### 2012: the ramen wave and the Japanese brands

Twenty years after Wagamama, ramen (ラーメン) came back as a dish in its own right. Bone Daddies in Soho, Tonkotsu (founded by Ken Yamada and Emma Reynolds) and Shoryu all opened in 2012. Then two Japanese chains arrived: Kanada-Ya and Ippudo opened almost opposite each other in Covent Garden in 2014, Ippudo's first site in Europe ([Londonist](https://londonist.com/2014/10/ramen-reviews-ippudo-and-kanada-ya), [OpenTable](https://opentable.co.uk/blog/?p=9476)). Both serve tonkotsu (豚骨), pork-bone broth from Kyushu.

The order matters. Japanese operators came after British ones had shown there was demand.

### Where the money came from

Roll-out needs capital, and these chains mostly got it from private equity: investment funds that buy a company, grow it with borrowed money and sell it on within a few years.

| Brand | Deal | Terms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| YO! Sushi | 2003: Woodroffe sells control, backed by Primary Capital | £10m deal ([YO!](https://yo.co.uk/simon-woodroffe/)) |
| Wagamama | 2005 stake to Lion Capital; 2011 sale to Duke Street | Terms not found this run (Wikipedia) |
| Wagamama | October 2018: bought by The Restaurant Group (TRG), owner of Frankie & Benny's | £357m cash plus £202m net debt, enterprise value £559m; 133 UK restaurants at the time ([Restaurant Online](https://www.restaurantonline.co.uk/Article/2018/10/30/The-Restaurant-Group-buys-Wagamama-in-deal-worth-559m)) |
| YO! Sushi | 2019: merges with US sushi group Snowfox | Telegraph put the cost at about US$100m ([Salmon Business](https://www.salmonbusiness.com/yo-sushi-merges-with-us-rival/)) |
| YO! / Snowfox | June 2023: bought by Zensho Holdings, Japan's largest foodservice company by sales | Valued at US$621m, about £494m ([The Caterer](https://www.thecaterer.com/news/yo!-sushi-restaurants-snowfox-sold-zensho)) |
| Wagamama (via TRG) | October 2023: Apollo takes TRG private | £506m, 65p a share ([Hospitality Ireland](https://hospitalityireland.com/restaurant/apollo-to-take-wagamama-owner-restaurant-group-private-for-506m-201171)) |

Enterprise value means the price for the shares plus the debt the buyer takes on, which is why the Wagamama deal is quoted as both £357m and £559m. Some shareholders balked at a price of more than 13 times earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA).

The result is scale. Wagamama had 161 UK sites at the end of 2023 with a target of 200 to 220 ([MCA via search](https://www.mca-insight.com/restaurants/wagamama-uk-lfls-up-82-in-q3/563981.article)). A Restaurant Online feature this week puts YO! at around 500 locations, including supermarket concession counters, and itsu at about 80 restaurants ([Restaurant Online](https://www.restaurantonline.co.uk/Article/2026/10/21/rolling-out-inside-the-uks-sushi-market/)). The YO! figure is not comparable with the "over 100" restaurants and kiosks reported in 2023, because it counts concessions; I give both and treat the 2026 one as the total estate.

### What this means if you look at it as a business

This is my reading of the facts above, not a sourced claim.

1. **The format was the product.** Wagamama, YO! and itsu each borrowed a service model from elsewhere (the canteen, the conveyor, the Pret counter) and put Japanese-style food in it. That made them easy to copy site by site, which is what investors pay for.
2. **Authenticity was not the barrier to entry.** British and Korean founders built the mass market; Japanese chains arrived once demand was proven. A Japanese brand entering now competes with incumbents that own the customer's idea of Japanese food.
3. **Value moved to the exits.** The founders made money early; most of the value was captured by funds trading the brands. Zensho's purchase shows Japanese capital now buys into the British market rather than building it.
4. **Grocery is the next channel.** itsu's sales growth is in supermarkets, and YO!'s count is swollen by concessions. Lesson 7 covers that trade.

### Key terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Kaiten-zushi (回転寿司) | Conveyor-belt sushi: plates pass diners on a belt and are priced by colour |
| Grab-and-go | Food packed in advance and sold for quick purchase, as at Pret, itsu and Wasabi |
| Ramen (ラーメン) | Wheat noodles in broth; the dish Wagamama's menu was built on and the centre of the 2012 wave |
| Tonkotsu (豚骨) | Rich pork-bone ramen broth from Kyushu, the style of Ippudo and Kanada-Ya |
| Izakaya (居酒屋) | A Japanese pub serving shared small plates; the model behind Zuma |
| Private equity | Funds that buy companies, grow them with borrowed money and sell them on |
| Enterprise value | The price of a company's shares plus its net debt |
| Concession | A counter run by one brand inside another business's premises, such as a supermarket |

quiz.q: What did Wagamama, YO! Sushi and itsu mainly sell that made them easy to roll out?
options: Japanese-trained chefs in every site
Imported Japanese ingredients unavailable elsewhere
A familiar service format with Japanese-style food in it
Licences from Japanese restaurant groups
quiz.why: Each borrowed a format (the canteen, the conveyor belt, the Pret counter) that worked without menu knowledge and copied easily. Imported ingredients sound plausible, but the expatriate importers already supplied those; what was new was the format.

quiz.q: Who founded most of the British chains that took Japanese food to the high street?
options: Non-Japanese founders such as Alan Yau, Simon Woodroffe and Julian Metcalfe
Japanese trading companies looking for new markets
The Japanese government's food export agency
Japanese chefs who had run expatriate restaurants in the City
quiz.why: Wagamama, YO!, itsu and Wasabi were started by founders who were not Japanese. The City restaurants for Japanese businessmen stayed small and discreet; they did not build the mass market.

quiz.q: Why is the 2018 Wagamama deal quoted as both £357 million and £559 million?
options: The price was cut after shareholders objected
One figure is in pounds and the other in dollars
£559 million included the later Apollo deal
£357 million was the cash for the shares; £559 million adds the £202 million of net debt taken on
quiz.why: The enterprise value counts the debt the buyer assumes as well as the share price. The currency explanation is tempting but wrong: both figures are in pounds.

quiz.q: What does the order of arrival in the 2012–2014 ramen wave suggest?
options: Japanese chains created British demand for ramen
Japanese chains such as Ippudo arrived after British-run ramen bars had shown demand
Ramen only became popular after supermarkets stocked it
Ramen bars replaced conveyor-belt sushi entirely
quiz.why: Bone Daddies, Tonkotsu and Shoryu opened in 2012; Kanada-Ya and Ippudo came to Covent Garden in 2014. It is tempting to assume the Japanese originals led, but in London they followed proven demand.

quiz.q: What did Zensho's 2023 purchase of YO! Sushi's owner show?
options: Conveyor-belt sushi had stopped growing in Britain
British private equity was barred from Japanese food chains
Japanese capital now buys into the British market that British founders built
YO! Sushi was always secretly Japanese-owned
quiz.why: Zensho, Japan's largest foodservice company by sales, paid about £494 million for a group built from a British-founded brand. YO! had been British-founded and fund-owned until then, so the idea of hidden Japanese ownership is wrong.
